title: FAIR v1.0 Assessment
description: A draft framework transcribing the FAIR Guiding Principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016; GO FAIR Foundation) — fifteen sub-principles across Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable, for assessing how well data, metadata, and the infrastructure serving them support machine- and human-actionable discovery and reuse.
aboutHtml:
The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship set out how to make data and metadata Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable — by both humans and machines. They were first published as Wilkinson, M., Dumontier, M., Aalbersberg, I. et al. “The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship.” Sci Data 3, 160018 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18, and are maintained and published today by the GO FAIR Foundation.

This tool's fair framework transcribes the fifteen FAIR sub-principles (F1–F4, A1/A1.1/A1.2/A2, I1–I3, R1/R1.1–R1.3) verbatim as each principle's text, taken from the GO FAIR Foundation's own published wording and cross-checked against the machine-actionable FAIR Vocabulary ontology (Tobias Kuhn and Michel Dumontier, CC BY 4.0), which defines the same fifteen sub-principles as its own FAIR-SubPrinciple individuals. The four sections (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) correspond to the ontology's top-level FAIR-Principle individuals (F, A, I, R). Only the criteria (compliant/progress/non-compliant) and improvementAction fields are this tool's own addition: the FAIR principles themselves describe essential aspects of good data stewardship without prescribing a pass/fail scoring mechanism, so these are one reasonable operationalisation of them for a self-assessment, not an official rubric endorsed by GO FAIR or the original authors.

principles.title: F1: Globally unique and persistent identifiers
principles.text: (meta)data are assigned a globally unique and persistent identifier

criteria.compliant: Every dataset and its metadata are assigned a globally unique, persistent identifier (e.g. DOI, Handle, ARK) that resolves reliably over time.
criteria.progress: Identifiers are used for some but not all datasets, or the identifiers used are not globally unique or not guaranteed persistent (e.g. a local database key or a plain URL with no persistence commitment).
criteria.non-compliant: Datasets and their metadata have no persistent identifier; they are referenced only by file paths or ephemeral URLs.

principles.improvementAction: Assign a globally unique, persistent identifier (such as a DOI) to every dataset and its metadata record, using a recognised PID service.

principles.title: F2: Rich metadata
principles.text: data are described with rich metadata (defined by R1 below)

criteria.compliant: Data are described with rich, standardised metadata covering context, quality, provenance, and content, giving enough information to judge fitness for reuse.
criteria.progress: Basic metadata exists (e.g. title, date, format) but lacks the richness needed to judge fitness for reuse.
criteria.non-compliant: Data are published with little or no accompanying metadata.

principles.improvementAction: Adopt a metadata schema that captures rich descriptive, contextual, and provenance information, and apply it consistently to every dataset.

principles.title: F3: Metadata explicitly include the data's identifier
principles.text: metadata clearly and explicitly include the identifier of the data they describe

criteria.compliant: Every metadata record explicitly and unambiguously references the persistent identifier of the data it describes.
criteria.progress: Metadata records exist but do not consistently or explicitly include the data's identifier.
criteria.non-compliant: Metadata records do not reference the identifier of the data they describe.

principles.improvementAction: Ensure every metadata record explicitly includes the persistent identifier of the data it describes, in a machine-readable field.

principles.title: F4: Registered or indexed in a searchable resource
principles.text: (meta)data are registered or indexed in a searchable resource

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data are registered or indexed in a searchable resource (e.g. a disciplinary or generalist registry, catalogue, or search engine), so they can be discovered independently of the hosting system.
criteria.progress: (Meta)data are searchable within their own repository but not indexed or registered elsewhere.
criteria.non-compliant: (Meta)data are not indexed or registered in any searchable resource, and can only be found if the exact location is already known.

principles.improvementAction: Register or index the (meta)data in a recognised searchable registry or catalogue relevant to the discipline or data type.

principles.title: A1: Retrievable by identifier via a standardised protocol
principles.text: (meta)data are retrievable by their identifier using a standardised communications protocol

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data can be retrieved by their identifier using a standardised, well-documented communications protocol (e.g. HTTP/HTTPS).
criteria.progress: (Meta)data can be retrieved, but only via an ad hoc or undocumented mechanism rather than a standardised protocol.
criteria.non-compliant: (Meta)data cannot be retrieved using their identifier at all.

principles.improvementAction: Make (meta)data retrievable via a standardised, documented protocol such as HTTP/HTTPS, resolving directly from the identifier.

principles.title: A1.1: Protocol is open, free, and universally implementable
principles.text: the protocol is open, free, and universally implementable

criteria.compliant: The retrieval protocol is open, free to use, and universally implementable, with no proprietary or paywalled dependency.
criteria.progress: The protocol is mostly open but has some barriers (e.g. requires a specific proprietary client, or a paid API tier for higher volumes).
criteria.non-compliant: The retrieval protocol is proprietary, closed, or requires payment to implement or use.

principles.improvementAction: Replace or supplement any proprietary retrieval mechanism with an open, free, universally implementable protocol.

principles.title: A1.2: Protocol supports authentication and authorisation where needed
principles.text: the protocol allows for an authentication and authorisation procedure, where necessary

criteria.compliant: Where access restrictions are necessary, the protocol supports a standard authentication and authorisation procedure; where no restriction is needed, access is open by default.
criteria.progress: Some access control exists but is implemented outside the retrieval protocol (e.g. manual email requests) rather than through a standard mechanism.
criteria.non-compliant: There is no mechanism for authentication or authorisation, and no way to grant appropriately restricted access where needed.

principles.improvementAction: Implement a standard authentication/authorisation mechanism within the retrieval protocol for any data that needs restricted access.

principles.title: A2: Metadata remain accessible after data are gone
principles.text: metadata are accessible, even when the data are no longer available

criteria.compliant: Metadata records remain accessible even after the underlying data are no longer available (e.g. due to embargo expiry, withdrawal, or loss), documenting that the data once existed.
criteria.progress: Metadata are usually removed or become inaccessible alongside the data, though this is not a deliberate policy.
criteria.non-compliant: Metadata are deleted whenever the underlying data become unavailable, leaving no trace of the dataset having existed.

principles.improvementAction: Adopt a policy and technical mechanism to preserve metadata records independently of the data's own availability.

principles.title: I1: Formal, shared knowledge representation language
principles.text: (meta)data use a formal, accessible, shared, and broadly applicable language for knowledge representation

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data are represented using a formal, accessible, shared, and broadly applicable knowledge-representation language (e.g. RDF, or a standard structured format with a public schema).
criteria.progress: (Meta)data use a structured format, but it is proprietary, undocumented, or not broadly shared across the community.
criteria.non-compliant: (Meta)data are represented only as free text or in an ad hoc, undocumented structure.

principles.improvementAction: Represent (meta)data using a formal, community-shared knowledge-representation language or a well-documented structured format.

principles.title: I2: FAIR-compliant vocabularies
principles.text: (meta)data use vocabularies that follow FAIR principles

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data use controlled vocabularies, ontologies, or thesauri that themselves follow FAIR principles (findable, accessible, well-documented, and reused by the community).
criteria.progress: Some controlled vocabulary is used, but it is locally defined, undocumented, or not itself FAIR.
criteria.non-compliant: No controlled vocabularies are used; terms are free text chosen without reference to any shared vocabulary.

principles.improvementAction: Adopt established, FAIR-compliant controlled vocabularies or ontologies relevant to the domain, rather than free-text or locally invented terms.

principles.title: I3: Qualified references to other (meta)data

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data include qualified references to other relevant (meta)data — links that specify the nature of the relationship (e.g. “isDerivedFrom”, “isPartOf”), not just an unqualified pointer.
criteria.progress: (Meta)data reference other (meta)data, but the relationships are unqualified (plain links or free-text mentions with no specified relation type).
criteria.non-compliant: (Meta)data contain no references to related (meta)data at all.

principles.improvementAction: Add qualified, typed references between related (meta)data records, describing the nature of each relationship.

principles.title: R1: Richly described with accurate, relevant attributes
principles.text: meta(data) are richly described with a plurality of accurate and relevant attributes

criteria.compliant: Meta(data) are richly described with a plurality of accurate and relevant attributes, giving reusers enough context to understand, trust, and correctly reuse the data.
criteria.progress: Meta(data) include some descriptive attributes, but not enough to confidently judge fitness for reuse.
criteria.non-compliant: Meta(data) carry minimal or no descriptive attributes beyond a bare identifier or filename.

principles.improvementAction: Enrich meta(data) with a plurality of accurate, relevant descriptive attributes (methodology, context, quality indicators, etc.).

principles.title: R1.1: Clear and accessible usage license
principles.text: (meta)data are released with a clear and accessible data usage license

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data are released with a clear, machine-readable, and accessible data usage licence, stating what reuse is permitted.
criteria.progress: A licence is mentioned but is unclear, not machine-readable, or hard to locate.
criteria.non-compliant: (Meta)data carry no usage licence or rights statement at all.

principles.improvementAction: Attach a clear, standard, machine-readable usage licence (e.g. a Creative Commons or other open licence) to every (meta)data release.

principles.title: R1.2: Detailed provenance

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data are associated with detailed provenance information describing their origin, processing history, and the parties responsible for them.
criteria.progress: Some provenance information exists (e.g. a creator name) but lacks detail on processing history or responsibility chain.

principles.improvementAction: Document detailed provenance for (meta)data — origin, processing steps, and responsible parties — using a standard provenance model where possible.

principles.title: R1.3: Meets domain-relevant community standards

criteria.compliant: (Meta)data meet the domain-relevant community standards (formats, vocabularies, quality expectations) recognised by the relevant research community.
criteria.progress: (Meta)data partially follow community standards, or follow standards from an adjacent but not the most relevant domain.
criteria.non-compliant: (Meta)data follow no recognised domain or community standard.

principles.improvementAction: Identify and adopt the domain-relevant community standards for (meta)data format, vocabulary, and quality in the relevant research field.
